newsitem.title: UK: Dlr little changed at Euro close, bounces off lows.
newsitem.headline: Dlr little changed at Euro close, bounces off lows.

text.p: The dollar closed little changed in Europe, lacking conviction to extend its rally but regaining poise on downticks, traders said.
Dollar/yen eased off highs amid talk that Kampo, the giant Japanese postal fund, would start hedging foreign bond risk.
But news that the U.S. current accout deficit reached record levels in the third quarter failed to unsettle the dollar.

"In the good old days the dollar would have taken this badly but since it's controlled by asset market flows now it had no negative impact," said Tais Knuthsen, international economist at First Chicago in London.
The current account deficit widened to $47.96 billion from a revised $40.21 billion in the second quarter.
Even though the current account news had no immediate impact on the dollar, Knuthsen said this was a potential bugbear for the health of the U.S. unit.
"But as long as foreign investors are eager to put money into U.S. assets, it's easy to finance that deficit," he said.
The continued recovery of U.S. stocks from last week's shake-out also underpinned the dollar, traders said.
At 1603 GMT the dollar was at 1.5545/55 marks and 113.24/30 yen compared with 1.5560/64 and 113.22/27 in late Europe Monday.
Reports about Kampo's hedging plans pushed dollar/yen off a high at 113.70 yen as a big Japanese securities house and a U.S. investment bank sold dollars for yen, traders said.

"Dollar/yen softened a bit amid those reports," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. The reports were in line with last week's Kampo announcement that it planned to use currency forwards soon to hedge holdings of foreign currency, he said.
Such a transaction would involve selling versus the yen the foreign currency in which the bond is denominated. Kampo is one of the world's largest investors.
With the dollar sidelined in European trading, the Swiss franc and sterling attracted attention.
The Swiss franc recovered off lows after a near brush with its 1996 low against the dollar at 1.3330 Swiss francs. But traders said Swiss franc weakness remained a key feature.
News of a 0.7 percent drop in third quarter Swiss GDP - the seventh drop in a row - underlined the weak Swiss franc trend.

"The market is still looking for further Swiss franc weakness," said Knuthsen. Comments on Monday by Swiss National Bank board member Jean-Pierre Roth welcoming recent developments in the franc's exchange rate, also weighed on the currency.
Mark/Swiss closed just below a fresh 30-month high at 85.47 centimes. Dealers said talk of a large mark sell order by a U.S. investment house around 85.50 had capped gains intraday.
Traders kept a close eye on further developments on the stability pact in the run-up to the European Union summit in Dublin on December 13/14.
But so far the foreign exchange market appears to be unfazed by reports of differences between France and Germany about the details of the pact.
"A lot of the fears of a soft euro if the pact is less stringent appear to exaggerated," said Meggyesi at DMG.

Mark/lira gained on a report that Germany Chancellor Helmut Kohl's CDU party is looking to stall Italy's ERM entry in 1999, but a trade-off guaranteee of admission in 2002 was seen as a lira positive. Mark/lira was at 986.60/90 versus 984.10/60.
Sterling failed to hold on to gains above 2.57 marks, made in overnight trade amid talk Japanese banks bought the pound as a provision for bad loans to Channel Tunnel operator Eurotunnel.

Analysts said banks appeared to have borrowed sterling to lend to Eurotunnel, but as the year draws to a close, they woud be left short of sterling and with positions which have to be covered. -- Astrid Zweynert London newsroom + 44 171 542 7792
